lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: Differences in Maturation of Crops in Different Soils and Seed Beds

pages.title: What you will learn
pages.body:
🎯 **By the end of this lesson you will be able to:**
- Observe and record the maturity stages of different crops grown in different soils and seed beds.
- Discuss the differences in maturity stages among the different crops on the different soils and seed beds.
- Compare and contrast the maturity stages of crops and seedlings in the community or school garden with others grown elsewhere.

pages.title: What is Crop Maturity?
pages.body: Maturity, in crop production, refers to the stage at which a crop has developed enough to be ready for its intended use, whether that use is harvesting the leaves, the fruit, the grain, or the whole plant. Different crops mature at different rates, and even the same crop can mature at a different pace depending on the growing conditions it experiences, particularly the type of soil and the type of seed bed it is grown on.

questions.q: Crop maturity refers to
o: The colour of the seed used to plant a crop
The stage at which a crop is ready for its intended use
The total number of seeds planted
The type of tool used to plant a crop
questions.e: Maturity, in crop production, refers to the stage at which a crop has developed enough to be ready for its intended use, whether that use is harvesting the leaves, the fruit, the grain, or the whole plant.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: How Soil Type Affects Crop Maturity

pages.title: How Soil Type Affects Crop Maturity
pages.body: Soil type strongly influences how quickly a crop develops, since soil determines how easily roots can spread, how much water and nutrients are available, and how well a young plant can establish itself. Crops grown in loamy soil, which balances water retention, drainage and nutrient availability well, generally mature at a steady, healthy pace. Crops grown in poor sandy soil, which drains quickly and holds fewer nutrients, often mature more slowly and may produce smaller yields, unless additional watering and fertiliser are provided. Crops grown in heavy clay soil may also mature more slowly if the soil becomes waterlogged, since poor aeration around the roots can restrict healthy growth.

pages.title: How Seed Bed Type Affects Crop Maturity
pages.body:
Seed bed type, studied in an earlier grade, also affects how quickly a crop matures, since different seed beds provide different amounts of loose soil, drainage and root space. Crops grown on well prepared ridges or mounds, which offer loose, well drained soil, often mature faster and more evenly than the same crop grown on a poorly prepared flat bed with compacted soil. Nursery beds, used to raise young seedlings before transplanting, are managed specifically to protect and speed the earliest stage of a crop's development, though the crop's overall time to reach full maturity is also affected by the conditions it experiences after transplanting into the main field.

[[pic:A comparison photograph or drawing showing three identical maize plants at the same number of weeks after planting, one grown in loamy soil looking tall and healthy, one grown in sandy soil looking shorter and slightly pale, and one grown in waterlogged clay soil looking stunted, with each plant labelled by its soil type.]]

Notice how the same crop, planted at the same time, can reach very different stages of maturity depending on the soil and seed bed conditions it experiences, which is exactly the kind of difference this lesson asks you to observe and record for yourself.

pages.title: Observing and Recording Maturity Differences
pages.body: Height, number of leaves, presence of flowers, and overall appearance are useful, observable features to record when comparing the maturity of crops grown under different conditions. Recording these features at regular intervals, such as weekly, for crops grown in at least two different soils or seed beds allows a clear, evidence based comparison to be built up over time, rather than relying on a single, one time observation that might not reflect the true pattern of growth.

pages.title: Comparing School or Community Garden Crops with Crops Grown Elsewhere
pages.body: Comparing the maturity of crops and seedlings grown in a school or community garden with similar crops grown elsewhere, such as on a larger commercial farm or in a different community, can reveal how much local soil, seed bed choice, and management practices influence crop development. Such comparisons often show that crops grown with well prepared seed beds, appropriate soil improvement such as added compost, and consistent care mature more reliably than crops grown without these advantages, reinforcing the practical importance of the soil and seed bed knowledge studied throughout this strand.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: Stages of Growth and Time to Maturity of Common Crops

pages.title: Stages of Growth and Time to Maturity of Common Crops
pages.body:
| **STAGE OF GROWTH** | **WHAT HAPPENS** |
|---|---|
| **Germination and seedling stage** | The seed sprouts and the young plant forms its first roots and leaves |
| **Vegetative stage** | The plant produces more leaves, stems and roots and grows quickly in size |
| **Flowering stage** | Flowers appear and pollination takes place |
| **Fruiting stage** | Fruits, pods, grains or tubers form and fill |
| **Maturity and ripening** | The crop stops growing and is ready for harvest. Grains become hard and dry, and fruits change colour |

| **CROP** | **USUAL TIME FROM PLANTING TO HARVEST** | **SIGNS OF MATURITY** |
|---|---|---|
| **Maize** | About 3 to 4 months | Husks turn dry and brown and the grains become hard |
| **Okro** | About 2 months to the first harvest | Pods are tender and snap easily a few days after flowering |
| **Tomato** | About 3 months | Fruits turn from green to red |
| **Cowpea** | About 2 to 3 months | Pods turn yellow or brown and dry |
| **Yam** | About 7 to 10 months | Leaves turn yellow and the vines dry up |
| **Cassava** | About 8 to 18 months, depending on the variety | Lower leaves fall and the soil cracks around the swollen tubers |
| **Plantain** | About 12 to 15 months | Fingers become full and rounded and the tips of the fruit dry |

These times are typical values. A crop on fertile loamy soil and a well drained seed bed with enough water reaches each stage earlier than the same crop on poor sandy soil, waterlogged clay or a hard, unprepared bed.

pages.title: Going further
pages.body:
> 💡 **Going further**

Farmers and agricultural researchers sometimes use maturity differences deliberately, planting the same crop in staggered batches on different seed beds or fields so that the harvest is spread out over a longer period rather than all becoming ready at once. This practical technique, informed by the very same principles studied in this lesson, helps farmers manage labour, storage and market supply more effectively.

questions.q: Staggering planting on different seed beds can help farmers
o: Guarantee identical maturity for every crop
Harvest everything on exactly the same day
Prevent any crop from maturing
Spread out harvest over a longer period
questions.e: Farmers and agricultural researchers sometimes use maturity differences deliberately, planting the same crop in staggered batches on different seed beds or fields so that the harvest is spread out over a longer period rather than all becoming ready at once.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: Uses of Crops at Different Maturity Stages

pages.title: What you will learn
pages.body:
🎯 **By the end of this lesson you will be able to:**
- Discuss and write the uses of each maturity stage of each crop identified.
- Categorise crops by their different maturity stages and uses.

pages.title: Why a Single Crop Can Have Multiple Uses
pages.body: Many crops studied in this strand are useful to humans not only when fully mature, but also at earlier stages of their development, since the plant's tissues change considerably in texture, taste and nutritional content as it grows. Recognising this allows farmers and households to harvest and use a crop appropriately at more than one stage, rather than waiting only for full maturity.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: Uses of Crops at Different Maturity Stages

pages.title: Uses of Crops at Different Maturity Stages
pages.body:
Maize, cassava, plantain and cowpea are four crops that illustrate clearly how uses change with maturity stage, as summarised in the table below.

| **CROP** | **EARLY (IMMATURE) STAGE USE** | **MID STAGE USE** | **FULLY MATURE STAGE USE** |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Maize** | Young cobs sold or eaten roasted as a snack | Soft, milky grain used to prepare fresh corn dishes | Dried, hard grain stored and milled into flour |
| **Cassava** | Young leaves harvested and cooked as a vegetable | Partly developed tubers, smaller and more tender | Fully developed tubers used for gari, fufu and starch |
| **Plantain** | Young, small fingers rarely harvested | Green, firm fruit used to prepare fried or boiled dishes | Ripe, sweet fruit eaten directly or used in desserts |
| **Cowpea (beans)** | Young, tender pods eaten whole as a vegetable | Partly filled pods with soft, immature seeds | Dry, hardened seeds stored and cooked as beans |

[[pic:A three panel diagram of a single maize plant at three different maturity stages, an early stage with a small green cob, a mid stage with a fuller, milky cob, and a fully mature stage with a dry, hardened cob, each panel labelled with its typical use.]]

Notice how the same crop passes through a series of recognisably different stages, and at each stage, the plant part in question is suited to a different, specific use, rather than only becoming useful once it reaches full maturity.

pages.title: Categorising Crops by Maturity Stage and Use
pages.body: Leafy vegetable crops, root and tuber crops, grain crops, and fruit crops are broad categories that can help organise how different crops are used across their maturity stages. Leafy vegetable crops, such as cassava leaves or amaranth, are typically harvested while still young and tender, since their leaves become tougher and less palatable as the plant matures. Root and tuber crops, such as cassava and yam, are usually left to reach a fuller stage of maturity before harvesting, since the edible tuber needs time to develop and store enough starch. Grain crops, such as maize and rice, can be used at an early, soft stage for fresh eating, or left to fully mature and dry for storage and milling. Fruit crops, such as plantain and mango, are often used differently depending on whether they are harvested green (firm) or left to ripen (soft and sweet).

lessons.title: Uses of Common Crops at Different Maturity Stages

pages.title: Uses of Common Crops at Different Maturity Stages
pages.body:
| **CROP** | **EARLY OR IMMATURE STAGE AND ITS USE** | **MATURE STAGE AND ITS USE** |
|---|---|---|
| **Maize** | Fresh green maize is boiled or roasted. Green stalks and leaves are fed to animals | Dry grain is used for kenkey, banku, porridge, animal feed and seed |
| **Cowpea** | Young leaves and green pods are eaten as vegetables | Dry seeds are used for stew, koose and as seed. The dry haulms are fed to animals |
| **Okro** | Tender green pods are used in soup and stew | Hard, dry pods supply seed for planting |
| **Cassava** | Young leaves are cooked as a vegetable | Mature tubers are used for fufu, gari, kokonte and starch. Stems are cut for planting |
| **Plantain** | Mature green fruit is used for ampesi, fufu and chips | Ripe fruit is used for kelewele, roasted plantain and tatale |
| **Tomato and pepper** | Mature green fruits travel well to distant markets | Ripe red fruits are eaten fresh or cooked |
| **Coconut** | Young green nuts give coconut water and soft flesh | Mature brown nuts give oil, copra and fibre |
| **Cocoa** | Unripe pods are left on the tree | Ripe yellow or orange pods are harvested and the beans are fermented and dried |

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: Importance of Knowing Crop Maturity Stages

pages.title: What you will learn
pages.body:
🎯 **By the end of this lesson you will be able to:**
- Explain the specific uses of each maturity stage of different crops to humans, other crops, animals and the environment.
- Explain how the knowledge of the maturity stages of different crops helps a farmer in crop selection, time of harvest, and other decisions.
- Compare different stages of maturity of crops identified in the community with those used in other places.

pages.title: Why Knowledge of Maturity Stages Matters
pages.body: Understanding exactly when a crop reaches a useful maturity stage is not simply academic knowledge, since it directly affects household nutrition, farm income, animal welfare and even the health of the surrounding environment. Building on Lesson 6, which described what a crop can be used for at each stage, this lesson evaluates why having that knowledge in the first place is genuinely important.

pages.title: Importance to Humans
pages.body: Knowing crop maturity stages allows households to plan meals around what is available fresh at any given time, harvest crops at the stage that provides the best taste, texture or nutritional value for a particular dish, and avoid wasting food by harvesting too early or too late. For farmers, this knowledge directly affects income, since selling a crop at the maturity stage most valued by buyers, such as fresh, milky maize during a local festival, can command a better price than selling the same crop once it has fully dried.

pages.title: Importance to Other Crops
pages.body: Some crop residues become useful to other crops only once a particular maturity stage has passed. For example, allowing a leguminous crop such as beans to fully mature and its roots to remain in the soil supports greater nitrogen fixation, benefiting a subsequent crop such as maize planted in the same field, as studied in Lessons 1 and 2 of this strand. Timing the harvest of one crop correctly can therefore have a knock on benefit for the crop planted after it.

questions.q: Allowing a leguminous crop to fully mature before harvest can benefit a subsequent crop mainly through
o: Increased soil nitrogen from root nodules
Increased sunlight for the next crop
Reduced rainfall for the area
Removal of all soil nutrients

pages.title: Importance to Animals
pages.body: Many crop parts become suitable animal feed only at particular maturity stages, such as maize stalks and cobs left over after grain harvest, or cassava peels generated during processing. Knowing when these residues become available, and in what condition, allows farmers to plan animal feeding schedules around crop harvests, making efficient use of materials that might otherwise be wasted.

pages.title: Importance to the Environment
pages.body:
Harvesting crops at the correct maturity stage can reduce environmental waste, since crops harvested too early may fail to develop properly and rot, while crops left unharvested too long may fall to the ground and decay without being used at all. Correctly timed harvesting also allows crop residues to be managed deliberately, whether ploughed back into the soil to support the next planting, or composted, rather than left to decompose in an uncontrolled way that could encourage pests or disease.

[[pic:A simple flow diagram showing a single crop maturity timeline with four branching arrows pointing to four labelled boxes, Humans (fresh food and income), Other crops (soil nutrients from residues), Animals (feed from residues), and Environment (reduced waste through correct timing), showing how one crop's maturity stage benefits all four areas.]]

Notice how a single, well timed harvesting decision can create benefits that ripple outward to humans, other crops, animals and the environment all at once, which is why understanding maturity stages is considered such valuable, practical knowledge.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: How This Knowledge Helps Farmers with Crop Selection and Harvest Timing

pages.title: How This Knowledge Helps Farmers with Crop Selection and Harvest Timing
pages.body: Farmers who understand maturity stages can select crop varieties suited to their local growing season length, choosing faster maturing varieties where the rainy season is short, or slower maturing, higher yielding varieties where conditions allow a longer growing period. This same knowledge helps farmers decide the correct time to harvest, avoiding losses from harvesting too early, when yield and quality are still low, or too late, when crops may spoil, be attacked by pests, or lose market value.

pages.title: Comparing Local Maturity Practices with Other Places
pages.body: Comparing how crops are grown and harvested at different maturity stages in your own community with practices used elsewhere, whether in a different region of Ghana or in other countries, can reveal valuable lessons. Some regions may have developed particular expertise in timing harvests for maximum market value, or in making use of crop parts at stages that are overlooked elsewhere, and learning from these differences can help a community improve its own practices.

pages.title: Going further
pages.body:
> 💡 **Going further**

Agricultural extension services in Ghana often provide guidance on recommended maturity periods and harvest timing for major crops, helping farmers apply this knowledge with data based confidence rather than guesswork alone. Learners interested in agriculture can benefit from engaging with such extension resources, alongside the practical, observation based knowledge developed throughout this strand.
